title: Use written communication in extension and development

lessons.title: Planning written communication for farmers and stakeholders
lessons.html:
Why writing matters in extension

Extension practitioners write every day: visit reports, farmer letters, information leaflets, WhatsApp messages to study groups, project proposals, minutes and articles for local newspapers or commodity magazines. Good writing saves time, avoids misunderstandings and builds credibility with farmers, managers and funders.

Know your audience and purpose

Before writing, answer three questions:

  1. Who will read it? A smallholder with limited schooling, a commercial farmer, a district manager or a bank.
  2. What must they know or do after reading? For example, bring cattle to the dip tank on Thursday, or approve funding for a borehole.
  3. How will they read it? On a cell phone, on a printed leaflet at the co-op, or in a formal file.

Choosing the right format

PurposeFormat
Record a farm visitVisit report or diary entry
Explain a practiceLeaflet, fact sheet or poster
Invite people to a meetingNotice, letter or SMS
Request funds or supportProposal or business plan
Record decisionsMinutes

Language choice

South Africa has many official languages. Write farmer materials in the language the farmers use most, and have translations checked by a fluent speaker who understands farming terms. Avoid jargon such as 'integrated pest management' unless you explain it in plain words. Use local terms that farmers know, such as camp, kraal or veld.

lessons.title: Writing clear reports, letters and leaflets
lessons.html:
Principles of plain writing

  • Put the most important message first.
  • Use short sentences and active voice: 'Dip the cattle every week' rather than 'Cattle should be dipped on a weekly basis'.
  • One idea per paragraph.
  • Use headings, numbered steps and bullet lists.
  • Give specific facts: dates, places, quantities, names.
  • For products, write 'follow the product label' rather than quoting dosages from memory.

Farm visit report

A good visit report includes: date, farm and farmer name, purpose of the visit, observations, advice given, agreed actions with responsible persons and dates, and the next visit date. Write it the same day while details are fresh. Reports form the record of your service and may be needed for audits or for a colleague who takes over.

Formal letters and emails

Use a clear subject line, a polite greeting, a short opening stating the purpose, the details, the action required and a closing with your contact details. Keep a copy on file.

Leaflets and fact sheets

  1. Choose one topic, for example preventing Newcastle disease in village chickens.
  2. Use a strong title and a few key messages.
  3. Use simple drawings or photos where possible, to support readers with limited literacy.
  4. Include where to get help, such as the local animal health technician or state vet.
  5. Pre-test the draft with a few farmers and revise it.

Digital messages

WhatsApp groups are widely used. Keep messages short, check facts before sending and avoid forwarding unverified rumours, for example about a disease outbreak. Respect privacy and do not share farmers' personal details without permission.

lessons.title: Proposals, minutes and editing your work
lessons.html:
Writing for development projects

Project proposals

Practitioners often help groups apply for support from government programmes, municipalities or donors. A typical proposal contains:

  1. Background: who the group is and the problem.
  2. Objectives that are specific and measurable.
  3. Activities and timeline.
  4. Budget in ZAR, showing what the group contributes.
  5. Expected results and how they will be measured.
  6. Management and sustainability plans.

Follow the funder's template exactly and attach the requested documents, such as registration certificates and bank confirmation. Do not exaggerate results; credibility is important for future applications.

Minutes of meetings

Minutes record the date, venue, attendance, apologies, matters discussed, decisions taken and action items with responsible persons and deadlines. They are not a word-for-word transcript. Circulate them promptly and have them confirmed at the next meeting. For co-operatives and associations, accurate minutes protect members when disputes arise.

Editing and proofreading

  • Read the text aloud; awkward sentences become obvious.
  • Check facts, figures, names and dates.
  • Remove repetition and unnecessary words.
  • Check spelling and grammar, but do not rely only on a spell checker.
  • Ask a colleague to read important documents before they are sent.

Professional standards

Always acknowledge sources when you use information from research institutions or other writers. Keep confidential farm information private. File written records so they can be found later.

Key points

  • Plan by asking who will read, what they must do and how they will read it.
  • Choose the right format and the farmers' preferred language.
  • Use plain language, active voice and the most important message first.
  • Write visit reports the same day and record agreed actions.
  • Edit, check facts and acknowledge sources before sending.

quiz.question: Which sentence follows plain writing principles?

options.text: Cattle should be dipped on a weekly basis
Weekly dipping of cattle is to be undertaken
It is recommended that dipping occurs weekly

quiz.question: When should a farm visit report ideally be written?

options.text: At the end of the month
The same day, while details are fresh

quiz.question: Which format is most suitable for recording decisions of a co-operative meeting?
What should a leaflet on a product-based practice say about dosages?

options.text: Use the dosage a neighbour uses
Leave dosage out and say nothing

quiz.question: Why should a leaflet be pre-tested with a few farmers?

options.text: To check that farmers understand it and revise it before wide use
So farmers can pay for it

quiz.question: Minutes should be a word-for-word transcript of everything said at a meeting.
It is good practice to avoid forwarding unverified rumours about disease outbreaks in farmer WhatsApp groups.
Which of these belong in a typical project proposal? (select all that apply)

options.text: Exaggerated results to impress the funder
Farmers' private ID numbers on the cover page
